title: KV cache eviction, paging & prefix reuse deep dive - Aurora Tech
summary: Redwood SE walked Aurora Tech through KV cache architecture and common eviction/paging scenarios. Discussed root causes for unexpected evictions during long-context chat sessions, prefix reuse implications, batching interactions, and on-prem/VPC constraints. Action items: run targeted repro, share eviction thresholds/config docs, schedule benchmark run in private VPC environment.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-04-20 08:30 PDT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Marcus (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Lena (Aurora Head of ML), Daniel (Aurora Infra), Rita (Aurora Security)

Summary (auto): Rapid technical deep dive focusing on KV cache eviction symptoms Aurora is seeing in long-context agent/chat sessions. Discussed paging, prefix reuse, and potential fixes including adjusted eviction policy, smarter prefix-keying, and batching window changes.

[00:00] Marcus: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we'll do a deep dive on the KV cache behavior you've been seeing. Priya will drive the technical side.
[00:18] Priya: Hi all. Quick note, feel free to interrupt — we know these topics get detailed. Lena, can you restate the main symptom you're seeing?
[00:28] Lena: Yeah so basically when our agents run 8k-12k context conversations we start seeing degraded completions after a while, and we noticed a lot of cache misses that look like evictions. It's inconsistent — sometimes it happens after a few user turns, sometimes after 100s of tokens.
[00:46] Daniel: To add, it's mostly on our private deployment (on-prem), single-region, GPU nodes with mixed batch sizes. We're seeing increased latency spikes and token regen.
[00:58] Priya: Got it. A couple immediate suspects: (1) eviction due to capacity under high KV allocations (long context + many concurrent sessions), (2) prefix reuse/pollution where slightly different prompt prefixes create many keys, (3) paging between GPU memory and host when KV memory pressure hits, esp on quantized models.
[01:20] Lena: We do reuse system prompts a lot but then append dynamic user history fragments. Could that explode the keyspace?
[01:28] Priya: Yes. If your prefix tokens differ even by a token, it often becomes a distinct KV entry. So reuse doesn't always hit unless prefix normalization or canonicalization is used.
[01:38] Marcus: Quick interjection — we published a doc on prefix canonicalization and key hashing, you'll get that after.
[01:44] Rita: From security side, we also need to ensure KMS and audit logs are preserved when we start tweaking cache behavior — can adjustments affect logs?
[01:52] Priya: Good point — cache tuning doesn't change audit trails. The cache lives in the runtime layer; audit/KMS for request metadata and encryption of persistent blobs remain unchanged. But we'll note any config changes as part of the security checklist.

[02:10] Priya: Let's walk through the typical lifecycle for KV entries — creation on first prefix generation, growth as tokens are cached, and then eviction policies: LRU-ish with heuristics that consider token cost and sequence length. On dedicated pools with huge concurrency we sometimes see fast churn.
[02:34] Daniel: Can you explain LRU-ish heuristics? We saw a config parameter called eviction_score in logs.
[02:40] Priya: eviction_score is a composite used by the runtime: recency*weight + token_count*size_penalty + model_layer_penalty. It's not purely LRU, it's more like weighted-LRU to prioritize keeping larger or more expensive prefixes depending on the profile.
[02:58] Marcus: This is also why different sequence lengths and model quantizations change behavior — quantized KV entries may use less memory but can change the eviction_score calculation.

[03:12] [03:15] Lena: What about paging — could that cause the latency spikes we see?
[03:19] Priya: Absolutely. When KV memory exceeds GPU allocation, runtime will page cold entries to host memory. That results in a high-latency token fetch when the entry is needed again. In our logs that looks like increased read latency and then eviction if memory remains under pressure. Paging frequency depends on GPU memory pressure and OS-level swapping in addition to runtime-level decisions.
[03:44] Daniel: We're on older NVIDIA drivers and a mixed GPU fleet. Could driver differences affect paging behavior?
[03:50] Priya: Yes — driver and CUDA runtime versions influence pinned memory and transfer throughput. Also on-prem NVLink topology matters for multi-GPU KV sharing. We'll need your driver versions and topology to be precise.

[04:10] Marcus: Let's talk about prefix reuse mitigation strategies. Priya?
[04:14] Priya: There are a few approaches: (1) canonicalize prefixes — strip/normalize variable tokens like timestamps or IDs; (2) bucket prefixes into coarse-grained keys for less cardinality; (3) TTL-based retention for low-value keys; (4) apply adaptive caching where stable prefixes get sticky reservations. Each has tradeoffs with accuracy vs cost.
[04:40] Lena: We'd be worried about canonicalization changing completions — does it reduce quality?
[04:45] Priya: Potentially. If you canonicalize too aggressively you lose nuance. We usually recommend a hybrid: canonicalize low-signal metadata but keep semantic content intact. We can run A/B tests on a small corpus to measure impact.

[05:05] [05:10] Daniel: Batching — could our batching window be colliding with cache expectations? We're using a 50ms queuing window on the serving tier.
[05:17] Priya: Batching interacts with prefix hash locality. Longer batch windows increase request aggregation which can help throughput but may reduce per-session cache hit locality if it mixes sessions. If you batch across many sessions, the runtime may evict less frequently accessed keys. Usually there's an optimal window per workload; 50ms is common but depends on concurrency and request size.
[05:43] Marcus: Also note we have features that do session-aware batching to preserve locality — we'll show that in the follow-up demo.

[06:00] Priya: Quantization note: 4-bit quantization reduces KV footprint but can change runtime memory alignment, sometimes leading to small increases in overhead for metadata. In tight memory conditions this can flip which keys are evicted first. So it's a factor, but not always primary.

[06:20] [06:25] Lena: On our side, what telemetry should we give you to repro?
[06:29] Priya: The best set: request traces with session IDs, token counts, timestamps; runtime eviction logs (we need the eviction_score snapshot ideally), GPU memory usage timelines, driver/CUDA versions, and a few sample prompts that trigger the symptom. If you can provide a sample failing session trace that reproduces the miss after X turns that's gold.
[06:52] Daniel: We can attach those; we'll scrub PII.

[07:00] Priya: Great. Now for on-prem specific items: ensure your pinned-memory settings and ulimit for locked memory are tuned. OS swapping can cause paging outside the runtime which is worse. Also check NVLink and interconnect saturation. We sometimes recommend raising the KV reserved pool on nodes with lots of long-context sessions.
[07:24] Marcus: We have a script to collect the staging node metrics — I'll share.

[07:32] Rita: Security question — if we change TTLs or bucket keys, does that change data residency or retention policy for audit?
[07:40] Priya: No; cache tuning is ephemeral runtime behavior. Persistent storage policies and logs remain governed by your retention configuration. We'll document that explicitly.

[07:52] [08:00] Lena: Any quick mitigations we can try before the follow-up?
[08:04] Priya: Three quick experiments: (A) reduce batch window to 20-30ms to increase session locality, (B) increase KV reserved pool by 10-20% on staging nodes, (C) run a canonicalization pass on low-value tokens. Run one at a time and measure.
[08:22] Daniel: We'll try A and B in staging tomorrow.

[08:30] Priya: We'll also run a controlled benchmark from our side replicating your workload shapes (mix of 4k/8k/12k sessions) in a private VPC to observe eviction pattern and paging. That should point to config deltas.

[08:45] Marcus: On the compliance side, we'll include a note about KMS and audit logs in the config doc.

[09:00] [09:15] Lena: One more thing — prefix reuse patterns: sometimes agents append session metadata like "session_id=xyz" to the system prompt. Could that cause high cardinality?
[09:25] Priya: Yes. Anything unique per session that ends up in the prefix will multiply keys. Use metadata headers or request-level fields rather than inline tokens where possible.

[09:42] Daniel: About metrics — what should we monitor to detect early eviction/paging issues?
[09:47] Priya: Key signals: cache_hit_rate (per-session), eviction_rate, avg_kv_read_latency, GPU_mem_utilization, host_swap_activity, and tail-latency percentiles for token generation. We'll share a dashboard template.

[10:10] Marcus: Quick demo reference — we have a "KV cache profiler" that can show top keys by eviction_score and heatmap of access patterns. We'll schedule a walkthrough in the follow-up.

[10:22] Rita: From security, please include what logs we need to retain to satisfy SOC2 reviewers — request IDs, timestamps, config changes.
[10:31] Marcus: Noted. We'll include an appendix with recommended retention windows and minimal fields.

[10:40] Priya: Ok let's go through a hypothetical timeline for remediation: 1) Customer sends traces and topology, 2) Redwood SE runs private VPC benchmark reproducing the issue, 3) We propose config changes and a small A/B test, 4) Run pilot in staging, 5) Roll to prod with rollback plan.

[11:02] Lena: Sounds good. Any CTAs on our side beyond traces?
[11:06] Daniel: We'll also export driver versions and CUDA logs.

[11:12] Priya: Perfect. I'll also attach our internal eviction thresholds doc and a short checklist for on-prem tuning.

[11:20] Marcus: Recap / next steps: Priya will run the repro and share results; Daniel will upload traces; Marcus will send the KV tuning doc and the prefix canonicalization doc; schedule a follow-up demo week of 2026-04-27.

[11:35] Lena: Thanks, this was super helpful.

[11:38] Marcus: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email with the artifacts and the scheduling link.

End of transcript.
